---
title: "Architecture"
subtitle: "Two engines, and the arrow that closes the loop"
---

## Why two systems

```
Volume ─▶ Lakebase ─▶ bronze ─▶ silver ─▶ model ─▶ gold ─▶ Lakebase ─▶ CRM
  CSV      Postgres      Delta     Delta            Delta   reverse ETL
                                                        └─▶ parquet ─▶ public app
```

**Lakebase** is Postgres 17 running inside Databricks: the operational side. Single
rows, foreign keys, low latency. It is where the retention team's system reads.

**Delta under Unity Catalog** is the analytical side. Columns, history, large
scans, time travel.

They are two engines because they solve two different problems. There is also an
operational reason: an analytical scan over the transactional database would
compete with the writes of the system that actually depends on it.

::: {.thread}
The predictions travel **back** to Postgres. A model whose output never reaches
the system that makes the decision has not finished.
:::

## The medallion layers, and the rule each one keeps

| Layer | What lives there | The rule |
|---|---|---|
| `bronze` | The source file, unchanged | Nothing is corrected here. Fidelity beats cleanliness |
| `silver` | Typed, clean, four derived features | Only **deterministic** features — nothing that learns a statistic |
| `gold` | Predictions and tables the app reads | One writer per table, no exceptions |

That middle rule is the anti-leakage control. Anything that learns from data —
scaling, encoding, imputation — lives inside the scikit-learn `Pipeline`, which is
fitted after the train/test split and inside each cross-validation fold. A scaler
fitted in silver would have seen the test rows, and every number reported
afterwards would be quietly optimistic.

## One writer per table

This one was learned the hard way. When two notebooks wrote the same table, every
re-run of the evaluation notebook wiped the Unity Catalog link the publication
notebook had added — and the only symptom appeared days later, when the
application stopped being able to load its model.

| Table | Written by | Read by |
|---|---|---|
| `silver.test_holdout` | notebook 04 | 05 |
| `gold.model_reference` | notebook 04 | 05, 06 |
| `gold.production_model_base` | notebook 05 | 06 |
| `gold.production_model` | notebook 06 | the app |

## Privacy enforced by the schema

`surname` exists in the landing table, because that table is a faithful copy of
the source. It does **not** exist in the modelled table.

The constraint is imposed by the schema rather than by the discipline of whoever
writes the next query. A column that does not exist cannot be leaked by accident,
and the boundary holds all the way to the operational query the CRM runs.

## The reverse ETL

```{python}
#| label: fig-quota
#| fig-cap: "The 800 contacts are not split evenly. Each country receives a share proportional to its expected churners, which is why Germany takes roughly the same quota as France with half the customers."
import charts
charts.country_quota()
```

The write back to Lakebase is append-only: one row per customer per scoring run.
That way what was predicted at a given moment can be reconstructed, instead of
overwriting the past. Both writes are idempotent — the run is upserted and the
predictions are deleted for that run before reloading — so running the cell twice
leaves the same state as running it once.
